question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=3 t-1,\qquad y=t^{3}+t,\qquad -\infty<t<\infty.
$$

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=-1.$

First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=-1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3 (-1)-1=-3-1=-4 \\ y & =(-1)^{3}+(-1)=-1-1=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(-4,-2).$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we need to find $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
x'(t)=3,\qquad y'(t)=3 t^{2}+1.
$$

So, we have

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}=\frac{3 t^{2}+1}{3}.
$$

At the point where $t=-1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{3 (-1)^{2}+1}{3}=\frac{4}{3}=\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $(x_1,y_1)=(-4,-2)$ and the slope $m=\frac{4}{3}.$ We get

$$
y+2=\frac{4}{3}(x+4).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ on the curve. Determine the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $x$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{6}=4+0+\frac{1}{6}=\frac{25}{6}, \\ y & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+2=0+2=2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(\frac{25}{6},2).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t(\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t}) \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi /2} & =\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{3}{4-0} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\frac{25}{6},2)$ and the slope $m=\frac{3}{4}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot (x-\frac{25}{6}).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $x$-axis when $y=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0-2 & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot (x-\frac{25}{6}) \\ -2 & =\frac{3 x}{4}-\frac{25}{8} \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(\frac{3}{2},\,0)$ is the $x$-intercept.

knowledge_point.title: Computing the Tangent Line to a Parametric Curve

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=t(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+3),\,y=\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=e^{2}$ on the curve. Determine the coordinates of the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis. Give exact answers.

The tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}},
{{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=e^{2}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =e^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡e^{2}+3)=5e^{2} \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡e^{2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(5e^{2},2).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡t+4,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{t}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{1}{t(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=e^{2},$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,e^{2}} & =\frac{1}{e^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡e^{2}+4)} \\  & =\frac{1}{6e^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(5e^{2},2)$ and the slope $m=\frac{1}{6e^{2}}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2=\frac{1}{6e^{2}}(x-5e^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =\frac{1}{6e^{2}}(0-5e^{2}) \\ y-2 & =-\frac{5}{6} \\ y & =\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(0,\,\frac{7}{6}).$
